extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, public-administration scholars, policymakers, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Developing and evaluating an agonistic democratic theory for the administrative state — i.e., institutional design principles and evaluative standards for agencies, rulemaking, participation, and judicial review that treat political conflict as permanent and politically valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict maintenance / 'unsettlement' as legitimacy metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Agonism seeks to build processes that unsettle decisions and promote friendly contestation over government policies, drawing the excluded back into a conflictual process of defining the dêmos anew. Legitimacy is found in sustained contestation rather than in settlement or broad acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design institutions and procedures so that decisions remain contestable and continually justified; favor practices that keep political disagreements alive in a non-antagonistic manner. Examples include procedural structures that compel periodic re-justification of settled policies and mechanisms that invite adversarial input rather than smoothing conflict away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisionality and contingency as sources of dynamism
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative rules and decisions should be provisional and contingent to enable dynamism in response to political contest and changing conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote rule designs and administrative practices that permit quick pivoting (e.g., temporary standards, sunsets, expedited reconsideration) so agencies can respond to ongoing contestation; accept more policy volatility as the tradeoff for greater democratic contest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminating barriers to changing policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce procedural and structural ossification that prevents agencies from changing policy in response to political contestation and shifting public preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reassess procedural requirements that make policy durable by default; consider streamlining rulemaking, enabling reversible or temporary instruments, and removing needless hurdles that lock in policy and foreclose contest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening the regulatory agenda
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow agenda-setting to be more open and accessible so a wider set of constituencies — especially marginalized groups — can place issues onto the administrative agenda and sustain contestation over priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create institutional pathways for nontraditional actors to influence agenda-setting (e.g., proactive solicitation, lower thresholds for docketing, special procedures for marginalized communities) rather than leaving the agenda solely to agencies or powerful interest groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardwiring conflict into administrative institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutional design should deliberately incorporate mechanisms that produce and sustain contestation (i.e., 'hardwiring' conflict), rather than relying on ad hoc disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement structural features (periodic review, mandatory cross-agency dissent, built-in adversarial procedures) that guarantee recurring, constructive contest about settled policies so political minorities can reengage and challenge outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nationwide injunctions and agonistic percolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial remedies (notably nationwide injunctions) and judicial intervention can spread and sustain contestation across jurisdictions — a dynamic the author calls 'agonistic percolation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the democratic function of broad judicial remedies not only in terms of legal correctness but also in how they influence the distribution and perpetuation of political contest; consider the agonistic payoff or harm when evaluating remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representational balancing and identity-conscious process
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative procedures should take identity, representation, and the inclusion of marginalized perspectives seriously, giving voice to groups that lack access to levers of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt identity-conscious participation mechanisms, targeted outreach, and procedural accommodations to ensure that contestation authentically reflects diverse constituencies rather than merely amplifying well-resourced interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flattening the bureaucratic hierarchy (diminished presidential primacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic legitimacy can be structured around a flattened bureaucratic hierarchy that fosters intra- and interagency competition rather than concentrating control in the President or a single hierarchical chain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reconfigure governance to make the President one competitor among many; accept shared or distributed authority inside the executive so political conflict among administrative actors contributes to democratic contest rather than being suppressible by a single actor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil-servant disobedience as a democratic instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil-servant disobedience can be tolerable or even necessary when presidential directives or executive actions would produce an illegitimate political remainder; civil servants have a role in resisting directives that would settle disputes improperly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate and sometimes tolerate civil-servant resistance where it sustains democratic contest and prevents premature or exclusionary settlements; this contrasts with views that treat disobedience only as an emergency last resort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice-and-comment and reason-giving (deliberative criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The conventional democratic justification holds that notice-and-comment and agencies’ duty to give reasons foster deliberation, alter preferences, and produce legitimacy through reasoned public engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that while notice-and-comment and reasoned explanations are important for deliberative legitimacy, they may fail in polarized contexts to produce broad acceptance; in agonistic design, these mechanisms should be repurposed to surface and sustain contest rather than to produce consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest-group marketplace / pluralist responsiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Pluralist accounts view administrative processes as marketplaces for influence where multiple interest groups vie to shape policy, which allegedly yields responsiveness to expressed preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat interest-group competition as a legitimacy channel but be alert to capture and resource asymmetries; under agonism, ensure marketplace dynamics do not exclude identity-based or marginalized claims and that competition remains contestatory rather than settling into capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral accountability / presidential control as legitimacy basis
rubrics_metrics.description: A conventional criterion grounds administrative legitimacy in electoral inputs — elections and presidential oversight serve as democratic settlement mechanisms for agency power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge limits: electoral settlement may be illusory in polarized, fragmented settings; agonistic design resists tying legitimacy exclusively to presidential control and treats elections as one input among many competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional fragmentation and the impossibility of unitary accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate administrative legitimacy by recognizing bureaucratic fragmentation (overlap, decentralization) that makes single-line accountability to the demos impractical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for fragmentation when assessing claims that agencies are or can be democratically controlled; fragmentation can be reframed as a feature under agonism because it sustains contestation, but it also complicates claims of representativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social-choice constraints on preference aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: Social choice theory shows that preference aggregation and coherent collective will are often impossible even under minimal assumptions, undermining expectations that administrative processes will generate settled, consistent democratic outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use social-choice insights to temper expectations about consensus-producing procedures; favor designs that accept incommensurable preferences and provide stable mechanisms for contest rather than attempting impossible aggregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of agonism sliding into antagonism
rubrics_metrics.description: A normative risk metric: institutionalized agonistic friction can morph into destructive antagonism that undermines democratic legitimacy if not carefully managed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor agonistic practices for signs of escalating hostility or delegitimation; set thresholds and safeguards to distinguish productive agonism from harmful antagonism and to deescalate when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural cost and regulatory-uncertainty tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Agonistic procedures impose real costs (administrative expense, slower decisionmaking) and may generate regulatory instability and uncertainty as policies remain contestable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh agonistic democratic payoffs against administrative costs; use empirical study (e.g., ACUS, GAO) to evaluate whether agonistic designs deliver democratic benefits that justify procedural burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-suitability test (when agonism is inappropriate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agonism may be unsuited to highly technical, safety-critical, or urgent domains (electric grid regulation, systemic financial risk management, national security) where instability imposes special harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess policy domain characteristics (technical complexity, systemic risk, need for stability) before applying agonistic reforms; reserve agonistic features for values-laden and identity-contested areas where democratic legitimacy gains are greatest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic, case-by-case and temporal evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the appropriateness of agonistic institutional features on a case-by-case and temporal basis — some questions and periods warrant more agonism than others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt flexible standards that consider the nature of the regulatory question, likelihood of antagonism, and changing social conditions; be willing to dial agonism up or down over time and across issue-areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unsettlement-for-flexibility tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: The administrative agon presents an explicit tradeoff: agencies may be permitted to act with fewer procedural constraints in exchange for institutionalized unsettledness and ongoing contestation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft explicit rules allowing procedural flexibility (e.g., expedited actions, temporary standards) contingent on stronger institutional guarantees of contestation and inclusion so that reduced procedural formality does not mean reduced democratic accountability.
